title: Saint Etienne's Farewell
summary: Sarah Cracknell reflects on Saint Etienne's history, their final album International and returning to Melbourne for a farewell performance. She also discusses the band's surprise at learning how their music helped Winona Ryder during a difficult film shoot.
transcript:
Sarah Cracknell of Saint Etienne spoke with Lauren Taylor from the UK, ahead of the band's farewell shows in Australia. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 13 August 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: After more than three decades of pop brilliance and 13 albums, Saint Etienne are preparing to say goodbye. Their final album, International, came out last year, with a bunch of collaborations, including the Chemical Brothers, Paul Hartnoll from Orbital, and Australia's very own Confidence Man.

You may recall a very sweet video doing the rounds on socials earlier this year: Winona Ryder told Elle magazine that, at the age of 20, while she was filming in Lisbon and going through quite a hard time, she randomly bought a Saint Etienne record from a street vendor, not knowing who the band were. She said they totally rescued her, and years later she wondered whether Saint Etienne were still together. The band replied to her that stranger things have happened, but we're glad we were there for you. And yes, we're still together.

I began my chat with Sarah Cracknell by asking what it was like to find out that the band had had such a strong impact on Winona Ryder.

Sarah: Well, we've dined out on that a lot, obviously. It's Winona Ryder, for flip's sake. We all love Winona Ryder. She's exceptional. Love her. And even though she's shoplifted, yeah, no, I think I did that in a sweet shop once when I was about 11. So we've all been there. Actually, I don't even know if she was done for that, so the jury's out. But that was amazing. I love that. We get lots of people saying that kind of thing, especially people like, I went to university and was introduced to your music, and it helped me in a difficult time, whatever that was, whether it was settling into uni, or something that had happened to them. It's really nice to be so useful. It's nice that we can make a difference to some people.

Lauren: Do moments like that make you think about the impact your music has for people, and ultimately what the songs are about?

Sarah: Very much so. We had a song way, way back called 'Archway People', and people moved to Archway, which at that point in time was a little bit sketchy. And I felt really guilty, because these people were like, I've moved to Archway from beautiful Italy. And you think, oh no, don't do that. It's lovely now, Archway; it's all been gentrified. But I think in a band you do have to have a certain amount of responsibility for what you say.

Lauren: Sarah, you've called this the goodbye tour, a happy-sad thing, more of a celebration than a wake. How is the band feeling heading into it?

Sarah: It's definitely more of a celebration. We wanted to go out on a high. I wanted to leave the Saint Etienne legacy intact. There are a couple of embarrassing moments, but not that many, and there could be more if we carried on, you know what I mean? There's a time, I think, when you have to just call it a day. And this is that time. But we wanted to go out and say a very grateful and thankful goodbye to all the fans we've had over the years. So it is a celebration.

But I don't know how I'm going to feel at the very last gig. We're doing a couple of festivals, and some gigs with Belle and Sebastian here, then a tour here in September, and then we're coming to you guys in New Zealand and Australia. Next year we'll do some more festivals, possibly a bit of Europe. But by the end of next year, that's it.

So when it comes to the very last gig, we're quite — especially me and Pete. Actually, Pete is the biggest crier in the band, and I'm next on the list. Bob isn't heartless; he just doesn't cry as much as we do. But I can feel it's going to be really emotional. It is emotional already, to be honest, but it's going to get worse.

Lauren: How did the conversations about wrapping things up unfold? Who was the first to go, hey, it's time?

Sarah: There's a dispute about that. I think it was me. Bob thinks it might have been him. And Pete just says, well, it definitely wasn't me. I don't know. We've always been very connected, in that we make records when we feel it's the right time, when we all get itchy feet and think, oh, it would be really good to go back in the studio for a bit and write some songs, or record some songs. So we've always been quite intuitive like that between the three of us, a bit witchy. And I think it's just the right time. It's just the right time.

Lauren: To rewind 35 years, for those who may not know, Pete and Bob originally started the band as a duo, and you joined as a permanent member slightly later. Can you tell me the story of how you met, and what you were up to just before you joined the band?

Sarah: I'd had my own band since I was about 15, and we never got a deal, basically. We put out a single and a 12-inch ourselves and stuff, and I thought, this isn't really going anywhere. It's really hard to get a deal. It was hard even then, and I think it's even harder now, to be honest. So I went to drama school, because when I was a little kid, I wanted to be an actress. I wanted to be Glenda Jackson or someone like that, a serious actress. So I'd done that, and I was doing some worthy fringe plays around London. And then, of course, Bob and Pete got in touch with me just at the point where I thought, I'm not going to be in a band anymore. That's what happened.

They came around for dinner, and then I went in to sing one song first, I guess, to see how it went. I sang 'Nothing Can Stop Us', which was the first single that came out with me on it. And we just really gelled, because we had very similar reference points growing up. We liked the same films, the same TV programs, the same music, the same bands. We liked vintage clothes. It was almost like I'd found my home, band-wise. It really did feel like that.

Lauren: When you look back on those early days, what do you remember? Have the dynamics of the way you work together changed since then?

Sarah: Oh, definitely. When I first joined, I didn't really do any writing with them, although I knew how to write; I'd written songs for my previous bands. But they had so many ideas already formulated in their back pockets, I'd say. So it took a little while for me to get involved in the writing. And I didn't want to come in all pushy. I'm not that kind of person. I'm a very laid-back person. So very gradually, I'd start adding bits, or changing lyrics so they'd flow better when I was singing. It was a really gradual progression.

And now we write, all three of us, and there are no egos about songwriting. We're very glad to have someone chip in and help out when you get stuck on, what, a third verse? I've got to write a third verse? You're kidding. I've already said everything I need to say. So we'll chip in and help each other out. It's a very organic process now, writing.

Lauren: You were saying your connection is almost witchy and spiritual, and you all seem like really great friends. Is there a secret to the band's longevity, do you think?

Sarah: I think, A, there are no egos, and we're very happy to share. It's quite difficult for bands where there's one key songwriter, or two, and they don't let the rest of the band in, because it's frustrating: you come up with ideas all the time, songwriting-wise and production-wise. If you're stuck in a band where that's not happening, you're going to get fed up. That's sometimes why bands split up, I think.

We get on really well. We laugh all the time. And I think the other reason we've been together for so long is that we haven't done lots of those massive year-long tours. That's going to be really challenging for people, getting on for that period of time, all exhausted, so we don't do that. That probably helps.

Lauren: You mentioned wanting to be an actress. You trained at drama school, and your dad, I understand, was Stanley Kubrick's first assistant director, which is pretty amazing. Does that background shape how you approach a song as a performer?

Sarah: Yeah, I think definitely in lyric writing, for all three of us actually; it's quite cinematic, and the music sometimes too. We write songs about characters. It's not autobiographical stuff: characters in a scenario, and you can leave a lot up to the imagination of the listener, because they can fill in the gaps themselves, which is great.

And growing up with my dad, who worked so hard: the film industry, especially then, was tough, with lots of being away from home for months on end. But I was lucky enough to go away with my dad quite a bit when I was really young. And just to see that — this is going to sound really naff, but there's a sort of work ethic. It's like everyone having one super objective, and that is to get the job done and get something amazing at the end of it. So I think I'm quite like that. I've got a good work ethic.

Lauren: Speaking of acting, Saint Etienne famously made a trio of films about London with the director Paul Kelly. What would you say the band's relationship to cinema is?

Sarah: Well, it's really strong, clearly: three films in. As a band, we're not just about the music. We like the whole aesthetic. For instance, all our sleeve design, we do everything; we're hands-on with that. Paul Kelly's done a lot of those sleeves, actually. We're very in tune with him, and we've worked so much with him over the years: pop videos, the films, sleeve design. So we're about the whole package. I always translate it to: we don't want to just make a wonderful sponge cake, vanilla with some cream and stuff in the middle, and leave someone else to ice it. We want to be in control of the whole way it's presented and the way it looks, as well as what's inside.

Lauren: I did want to talk to you about your latest record, too. There's a strong Australian connection on the new album: 'Brand New Me', a collaboration with Confidence Man, which I think started as a song they wanted you on, but ended up as yours instead. Is that right? How did it come together?

Sarah: Yeah, that's right. They got in touch with me via Danny at Heavenly Records, asking if I'd like to come and sing on something with them. So we started collaborating on 'Brand New Me', and then they really took off here, and I think they just got really busy, basically, so it went on the back burner for a bit. Then when we were doing this album, International, I thought, oh, that would be good on this. Because International is, like we were saying, a really celebratory, fun, uptempo party vibe, and I thought 'Brand New Me' would fit perfectly on it. So I went to them and said, is that all right? And they were like, of course.

Lauren: You've said Confidence Man left your jaw on the floor when you saw them live. What is it about their songs and performances?

Sarah: I think it's everything, but the performances are mind-blowing, aren't they? They're so good. I've seen them a few times. The one where it really was jaw-dropping was at the Brixton Academy in London. I was on the balcony bit, and everyone on the balcony was jumping up and down, and I was suddenly really concerned the whole thing was going to collapse. I was like, oh my God, I'm going to die. But everywhere in the Brixton Academy was just going crazy. They're so brilliant. Everyone should go and see them, everybody.

Lauren: You touched on this before: International is joyful and loud, coming right after The Night, which was more quiet and ambient. What's the relationship between those two records? And did choosing the loud, energetic record as the last one feel like the right way to say goodbye?

Sarah: Yeah, it is the way to say goodbye. It almost feels like a full circle for me, or half circle, semi-circle, or like bookends. Because the first record, Foxbase Alpha, was quite eclectic, with lots of ideas. If you listen to it, you might go, it's not cohesive. But it is. It was like a melting pot of ideas, I think that's what I'm getting to. And I think International is like that as well, especially because we've had so many collaborations on it, with the Chemical Brothers and Erol Alkan and various. So it felt very full — half circle, to me.

Lauren: You mentioned the collaboration with Erol Alkan, and you also worked with Paul Hartnoll from Orbital on the record. You've said they both brought ideas that just fit together, and that it felt spooky. Was there a sense of destiny around the record?

Sarah: Yeah, definitely. It was serendipitous, if that's the right word. Everyone we approached said, that's interesting that you've approached me, because I actually have this track I'm working on, or that I did a little while ago. When I spoke to Tom from the Chemical Brothers, he was like, well, I've been working on this track with Jez from Doves, who I know as well, and we kept saying in the studio, this sounds like a Saint Etienne track. It's like, send it over. So he sent it over, and we were just so excited. Everything fell into place. Again, witchy. We're a witchy, spooky band, I think.

Lauren: We're very excited to have Saint Etienne back in Australia and in Melbourne, even though it's for the very last time: a bittersweet tour, this one. You first played in Melbourne in 1998, at the Hi-Fi Bar, which is now Max Watt's. Can you tell us about that first time in the country, and any places that stood out to you?

Sarah: It's the first and only time I've been to Australia. We'd come from somewhere else, I think, maybe America or something, I can't remember. So we were quite out of it, exhausted from lots of flying, and we were tired anyway from doing some gigs. And it's really obvious, but seeing things like Sydney Harbour and the Sydney Opera House was like, oh my God. In Melbourne we were a bit more chilled. We were like, okay, we're here. It's really good. I remember we were very food-based, in that we were so tired, and we were trying to find things we could eat that pepped us up and gave us more energy. What are they called? Moreton Bay bugs. We were eating those a lot, even though they look like something terrifying and prehistoric, or Egyptian, what are those things called in Egypt, those beetles, scarab beetles or whatever. We ate a lot of those. And there was a lot of wheatgrass around, which there wasn't so much of over here in the UK. So we were gunning wheatgrass all the time, trying to stay awake.

Lauren: Amazing. I think you called that tour more of a fact-finding mission. What were you finding out?

Sarah: I guess whether people wanted us to come. Like I said, it's the only time we've been, so you never know whether people really want you to come or not. And we were so well received. The gigs were great. So we thought, oh, we do have an audience here that likes us.

Lauren: For anyone coming to the final Saint Etienne shows at the Forum here in November, would you mind sharing a little about what you've got planned for the farewell shows?

Sarah: Yeah, so they're a deep dive into all the old singles, all the fans' favourite songs. So again, they're mainly upbeat, dancey, party vibe: fan favourites and singles. And, like I said, a couple of deep-dive songs that we haven't played for so long, but we know the fans like them. I'm not going to tell you which ones, though, not yet. Surprise.

Lauren: We're very much looking forward to the tour at the end of the year. Thank you so much for all of the incredible music, and thanks so much for joining me, Sarah.

Sarah: Thank you. It's been fun.
